title: Mixed Synchronicity and the Limits of Instructional Design
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill responds to an OLC Insights article by Nicole Weber on whether asynchronous online courses need synchronous sessions. He welcomes her flexibility-minded principles but argues the piece shows a wider problem in instructional design, the assumption that designers can know in advance which interactions will matter. He points to the ADDIE framework, whose structure makes overplanning look virtuous and can turn completed templates into a proxy for quality. Using his own earlier suggestion of student-organized synchronous discussions, he argues that good design can create conditions for learning without prescribing everything that happens. Generative AI sharpens the point, because probabilistic systems can respond to needs designers could never enumerate. The consequence, he says, is less control over the learning path paired with far more rigor in assessing whether students have actually learned.
points: Student preference for asynchronous courses does not mean students want exclusively asynchronous experiences, as surveys from Wiley and Risepoint have shown.
ADDIE and similar frameworks encourage an a priori mindset in which completing objectives, alignment and templates stands in for evidence that learning occurred.
Good design can set up conditions for learning, such as student-organized discussions, without prescribing every interaction, and unplanned outcomes can still be valuable.
Generative AI can respond to unexpected questions and exploration, challenging the assumption that every useful learning interaction must be specified in advance.
Loosening control of the learning path must come with greater rigor in assessment, including credible evidence of mastery and willingness to intervene.
quotes: Student preference for asynchronous courses does not mean students want exclusively asynchronous experiences.
The problem isn't simply how ADDIE gets implemented. Its structure makes overplanning appear virtuous.
Going through the motions of instructional design is not evidence that learning occurred.
Sometimes good design means creating the conditions for learning without prescribing everything that happens.

Generative AI changes that equation. These probabilistic systems can respond to unexpected questions, support exploration, and navigate learning needs that designers could never fully enumerate beforehand.
We should be less prescriptive about how students learn and far more demanding about demonstrating what they have learned.
Less control over the learning path should come with more rigor in assessing learning outcomes.
